title: Xeroderma Pigmentosum: The Ophthalmic Guardian's Guide
summary: Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis characterized by a defect in Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER), leading to extreme UV sensitivity. For the ophthalmologist, it presents a relentless challenge of managing recurrent ocular surface neoplasia and progressive adnexal destruction.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Xeroderma Pigmentosum (XP) is a heterogeneous group of DNA repair disorders. The primary defect lies in the Nucleotide Excision Repair (NER) pathway, which is responsible for removing pyrimidine dimers (cyclobutane dimers and 6-4 photoproducts) caused by UV radiation. This leads to a 10,000-fold increase in the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer and a 2,000-fold increase in melanoma before age 20.

Classic skin findings; usually no neurological signs.
Associated with Trichothiodystrophy (TTD) and Cockayne Syndrome.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The DNA Repair Failure
content: Step 1: UV-B (290-320nm) radiation causes DNA cross-linking (Thymine Dimers).
Step 2: Defective NER proteins fail to recognize or excise the damaged segment.
Step 3: DNA polymerase bypasses damage during replication, inducing mutations (C to T transitions).
Step 4: Accumulation of mutations in P53 and RAS oncogenes leads to uncontrolled apoptosis or carcinogenesis.

sections.title: Dermatologic Triad
content: Acute Sun Sensitivity: Severe sunburn/erythema with minimal exposure in infancy.
Cutaneous Poikiloderma: Diffuse pigmentation, telangiectasia, and atrophy (freckle-like lentigines).
Neoplasia: Early onset Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC), and Malignant Melanoma (MM).

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations: Eyelids & Adnexa
content: Eyelid Lentigines: Multiple dark brown pigmented macules.
Atrophy & Cicatrization: Leads to Ectropion (eversion) or Entropion (inversion).
Madarosis: Complete loss of eyelashes due to chronic inflammation or tumor.
Neoplasms: Frequent BCC and SCC of the lid margins; high risk of orbital invasion.

sections.title: Ocular Manifestations: Anterior Segment
content: Conjunctival Hyperemia: Chronic 'red eye' from UV-induced inflammation.
Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN): High frequency of carcinoma in situ.
Corneal Xerosis: Severe dry eye due to tear film instability and lid malposition.
Corneal Scarring & Vascularization: Progressive opacification/pannus (pterygium-like).
Corneal Perforation: Resulting from thinning or aggressive neoplasia.

rows: Dwarfism, 'bird-like' facies, retinal pigmentary degeneration; NO skin cancer.
Poikiloderma, juvenile cataracts, radial limb defects.
Telangiectatic erythema, growth retardation, high risk of leukemia.
Brittle sulfur-deficient hair, ichthyosis, intellectual disability; variable UV sensitivity.
Pellagra-like rash, aminoaciduria, triggered by diet/stress.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. Clinical Examination: Family history (consanguinity) and skin/eye findings.
2. Functional Assays: UDS (Unscheduled DNA Synthesis) in cultured skin fibroblasts.
3. Comet Assay: Measures DNA strand breaks.
4. Molecular Genetic Testing: Multi-gene panels for XPA-XPG and POLH.
5. Histopathology: Biopsy of any suspicious ocular surface or eyelid lesions.

sections.title: Management: The Protective Protocol
content: Phase 1: Total UV Avoidance: UV-blocking films on windows, 100% UV-wrap sunglasses, wide-brimmed hats, and face shields.
Phase 2: Medical Prevention: Oral Isotretinoin (0.5-1.5 mg/kg/day) to reduce skin cancer frequency; Topical T4N5 liposome lotion.
Phase 3: Ocular Care: Frequent preservative-free lubricants, bandage contact lenses for exposure, and moisture chambers.
Phase 4: Neoplasia Surveillance: Full ophthalmic and dermatologic exams every 3 months for life.
Phase 5: Early Excision: Wide surgical excision of tumors with margin control (Mohs for lids).

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral
content: New enlarging pigmented lesion on conjunctiva (Possible Melanoma).
Chronic non-healing lid ulcer (Suspect SCC/BCC).
Rapidly progressive corneal thinning or white plaque (OSSN).
Sudden loss of vision or severe pain (Corneal Perforation).

content.explanation: UV sensitivity, Vascularization of cornea, Recessive inheritance, Eyelid tumors, Pigmentary changes, Ataxia/Neurology, IRrepairable DNA damage.

sections.title: Surgical Pearls for the Ophthalmologist
content: Cryotherapy: Useful for conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) adjunct.
No-Touch Technique: Vital during excision of OSSN to prevent seeding.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting: For reconstruction after large ocular surface excisions.
Lid Reconstruction: Prioritize protecting the globe; avoid tension that worsens ectropion.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam High-Yields
content: Most common ocular tumor in XP: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC).
Avoidance of UV must include artificial sources: Certain fluorescent lights and halogen lamps emit UV.
XP-Variant (XP-V): Patients have normal NER but a defect in translesion synthesis; they present later in life.
The cornea in XP often mimics 'severe chronic actinic keratitis'.
